title: Gas After Drinking Alcohol: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why alcohol gives you gas and bloating, which drinks are worst, why it shows up the next morning, how to get relief, and when gas after drinking needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Why does alcohol give you gas? How carbonation and fermentation cause gas after drinking, the worst drinks, quick relief, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** gas after drinking alcohol is common and, for most people, harmless. It usually comes from four things working together: the bubbles you swallow in beer, seltzer, sparkling wine, and soda mixers; the sugars and starches in drinks and bar food that your gut bacteria ferment into gas hours later; the way alcohol irritates the gut lining and changes how quickly food moves through; and the extra air you gulp when you drink fast, talk a lot, or smoke. Burping during the night is mostly the bubbles. Farting and bloating the next morning is mostly fermentation. The good news is that both are easy to cut down once you know which one you're dealing with.

**The quick rules:** If you get gassy every time you drink, switch from beer and sugary bubbly mixers to a still drink (wine, or a spirit with still water or juice), slow down, and skip creamy cocktails if dairy bothers you. The next morning, a short walk, plain water, bland food, and an over-the-counter simethicone product for trapped bubbles are reasonable first steps. If gas comes with severe or worsening belly pain, a swollen hard stomach, vomiting, blood, or black stools, stop treating it as a hangover and get checked.

> **When to see a doctor.** Gas after a night out is normally just uncomfortable. **Get medical care promptly if** you have severe belly pain that doesn't ease after passing gas, pain that spreads to your back (especially with vomiting, which can be a sign of pancreatitis), a swollen and hard abdomen, you can't pass gas or stool and you're vomiting, you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, your stool is black, tarry, or bloody, or you have a fever. **Book a regular appointment if** gas and bloating happen even after one or two drinks, you have diarrhea that lasts more than a couple of days, you're losing weight without trying, or your bowel habits have changed for several weeks. In an emergency, call 911. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Alcohol Gives You Gas: The Short Explanation

Gas in your gut comes from two places. The first is air and carbon dioxide that you swallow. The second is gas made inside you, mostly by the trillions of bacteria in your large intestine as they break down food your small intestine didn't absorb. A night of drinking tends to increase both at the same time.

Here's how the main causes line up:

| Cause | What it does | When you notice it | Biggest culprits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carbonation | Puts carbon dioxide straight into your stomach | During drinking and soon after (burping, fullness) | Beer, hard seltzer, sparkling wine, cola and tonic mixers |
| Fermentation | Gut bacteria break down sugars and starches you didn't absorb, releasing gas | Late at night and the next morning (farting, bloating) | Beer, cider, sweet cocktails, rum and cola, bar food |
| Gut irritation | Alcohol irritates the stomach and intestine lining and disturbs normal digestion | Next day, often with loose stools | Large amounts of any drink, drinking on an empty stomach |
| Swallowed air | Gulping, talking, straws, smoking, and vaping all pull air into your stomach | During the night (burping) | Fast drinking, drinking games, smoking |
| Specific intolerances | Lactose, fructose, gluten, or histamine sensitivity add their own gas and bloating | Hours later | Creamy cocktails, cider, beer, some wines |

Most people have more than one of these going on. A typical "gassy" night might be four beers, a basket of fries, and a late slice of pizza. That's carbonation, fermentable starches from the beer, more starch from the food, and an irritated gut, all at once.

## Carbonation: The Bubbles You Drink

Carbonated drinks are just liquid with carbon dioxide dissolved under pressure. When that liquid warms up in your stomach, the gas comes out. Most of it leaves the way it came in, as burps. Some of it moves further down and can add to bloating and wind.

Alcohol makes the burping part more noticeable for a simple reason. It relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, the ring of muscle at the top of your stomach that normally keeps stomach contents where they belong. A relaxed valve lets gas escape upward more easily, which is why beer burps can come with a sour taste or a bit of acid. If that sounds familiar, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers the acid side of the story in more detail.

Drinks ranked roughly from most to least bubbly in practice:

- **Beer** is carbonated and you usually drink a lot of it by volume. A pint is a lot of liquid and a lot of gas compared with a single glass of wine.
- **Hard seltzer and canned cocktails** are often more fizzy than beer, and people drink them quickly because they taste light. Our piece on [hard seltzer hangovers](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why "light" doesn't always mean easy on the body.
- **Sparkling wine, prosecco, and champagne** are highly carbonated, though the serving size is smaller.
- **Mixed drinks with soda, tonic, ginger ale, or energy drinks** add carbonation on top of whatever spirit you chose.
- **Still wine and spirits served neat, on the rocks, or with still water or juice** add very little gas from bubbles.

If your main complaint is burping and an uncomfortably full, tight stomach during the evening, carbonation is the first thing to change. Switching even half of your drinks to still options usually makes a noticeable difference.

## Fermentation: Why the Gas Shows Up the Next Morning

Gas that arrives late at night or the next day, especially farting, a rumbling belly, and bloating low down, is mostly produced in your colon. Your small intestine absorbs most of the sugars and starches you eat and drink. Whatever slips past it reaches the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it and release hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and in some people methane. That's normal digestion, and everyone does it. Drinking tends to send more fermentable material down the line than usual.

**Beer is the classic example.** Brewing turns most of the grain's starch into alcohol, but not all of it. Beer still contains leftover carbohydrates, including longer sugar chains that your body doesn't digest well. Heavier, maltier, and sweeter styles generally carry more of these than light lagers. Beer also contains some yeast residue, especially unfiltered and bottle-conditioned styles. Put several pints of that through your gut and your bacteria have plenty to work with.

**Cider and sweet drinks bring fructose.** Apples and pears are naturally high in fructose, and many ciders keep a lot of that sweetness. Plenty of mixers are sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup. A large share of adults absorb fructose poorly when they take in a lot of it at once, and the unabsorbed portion gets fermented. If rum and cola or a sweet cider reliably leaves you bloated, fructose is a likely suspect.

**Bar food and late-night food add to the pile.** Fries, pizza, burgers, wings, nachos with beans, and onion rings are full of starch, fat, and in some cases onion, garlic, and beans, which are well-known gas producers on their own. Alcohol lowers your inhibitions around food, so you tend to eat more of it, later, and faster than usual.

**Alcohol also changes how well you absorb things.** Drinking, particularly heavy drinking, can irritate the lining of the small intestine and disturb the normal rhythm of digestion. When absorption isn't working at its best, more undigested food ends up in the colon, which means more fermentation and more gas.

## How Alcohol Affects Your Gut Lining and Bacteria

Beyond bubbles and sugars, alcohol itself acts on the digestive tract. A few effects are well established:

- **It irritates the stomach lining.** Alcohol, especially in larger amounts or on an empty stomach, can inflame the stomach lining. That's part of why you might feel queasy, crampy, or "off" the next day. Our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) goes through the different kinds of pain and what they usually mean.
- **It changes how fast things move.** Alcohol can speed up parts of the gut and slow down others. Faster movement through the intestines leaves less time to absorb water and nutrients, which is linked to the loose stools many people get after a big night. If that's your main issue, see our article on [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking).
- **It affects your gut bacteria.** Research on heavier drinkers has linked regular high alcohol intake to changes in the mix of gut bacteria and to bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine, a condition in which bacteria that normally live further down settle higher up and ferment food earlier. That's a pattern seen with regular heavy drinking, not a single night out. Still, it helps explain why some people who drink often find they're gassy and bloated most of the time. We cover the bigger picture in our guide to [gut health and alcohol](/never-hungover/gut-health-alcohol-microbiome-protection).

For the typical social drinker, these effects are short-lived. The gut lining recovers and digestion settles down within a day or two of stopping.

## Swallowed Air: The Cause People Forget

A surprising amount of gas, especially the kind that comes out as burps, is just air. Doctors call swallowing excess air aerophagia. Nights out are full of habits that increase it:

- Drinking quickly or chugging
- Talking and laughing while you drink
- Drinking through a straw
- Smoking or vaping
- Chewing gum, which many people do on the way home
- Drinking from a can or bottle, which tends to pull in more air than a glass

None of this is harmful, but it adds up. If you mostly burp rather than fart, slowing down and pouring your drink into a glass can help as much as changing what you drink.

## Smelly Gas After Drinking

Most of the gas your gut makes, such as hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane, has no smell. The odor comes from small amounts of sulfur-containing gases that bacteria produce when they break down certain foods. So if your gas smells worse after a night out, the usual explanation is what you ate alongside the alcohol, plus more fermentation overall.

Common contributors:

- **Protein- and sulfur-rich foods** like red meat, eggs, cheese, and processed meat
- **Onions, garlic, and cruciferous vegetables** such as broccoli and cabbage
- **Beer**, which can contain sulfur compounds from brewing and gives bacteria extra material to ferment
- **Gut irritation and faster transit**, which can change the mix of what reaches the colon

Strong-smelling gas on its own is not a sign of anything serious. If it's paired with greasy, pale, floating stools that are hard to flush, ongoing diarrhea, or weight loss, mention it to a doctor, because that pattern can point to a problem absorbing fat.

## Gas and Bloating After Drinking: Is It Gas or Water?

"Bloating" can mean two different things, and it helps to know which one you have.

**Gas bloating** feels like pressure inside your belly. Your stomach may look rounder, it may gurgle, and the feeling often eases after you burp or pass gas or go to the bathroom. It tends to get worse through the day as you eat.

**Water retention** feels more like general puffiness. Your face, fingers, or ankles look swollen, rings feel tight, and your belly may look soft rather than tight. That's more about salt, dehydration, and inflammation than gas. Our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) explains that side of things.

Plenty of people get both at once after a night of beer and salty food. The fixes overlap (water, a walk, lighter food), but simethicone and other gas remedies only help the first kind.

## Which Drinks Cause the Most Gas?

Everyone's gut is different, but this is a reasonable general ranking based on carbonation, leftover sugars, and typical serving sizes:

1. **Beer, especially heavy, sweet, or unfiltered styles.** Carbonation plus fermentable carbohydrates plus large volumes.
2. **Cider.** Carbonated and often high in fructose.
3. **Sweet carbonated cocktails** (rum and cola, vodka and energy drink, anything with soda or syrups).
4. **Hard seltzers and canned cocktails.** Very fizzy, though usually lower in sugar.
5. **Sparkling wine.** Fizzy, but smaller servings.
6. **Creamy cocktails** like White Russians, mudslides, and cream liqueurs, if you're lactose intolerant.
7. **Still wine.** Low carbonation, though sweet wines carry more sugar.
8. **Spirits neat, on ice, or with still water or soda water in small amounts.** The least likely to cause gas from the drink itself.

A note on soda water: it has no sugar, but it's still carbonated. If burping is your problem, a vodka soda isn't as gas-free as people assume. A spirit with still water, a splash of juice, or on ice is the lowest-gas option.

## Gas From Beer Specifically: Gluten, Yeast, and Style

Beer comes up so often with gas that it deserves its own section.

**Gluten.** Most beer is made from barley, which contains gluten. If you have celiac disease, beer can cause bloating, gas, diarrhea, and pain, along with damage to the small intestine. Some people without celiac disease also report gut symptoms from wheat and barley products. If beer consistently bothers you but wine and spirits don't, it's worth asking a doctor about celiac testing, ideally before you cut gluten out, since going gluten-free first can make the test less reliable.

**Yeast and unfiltered beers.** Hazy IPAs, wheat beers, and bottle-conditioned ales carry more yeast and suspended material. Some people find these sit heavier and cause more wind than clear lagers.

**Style and strength.** Rich, malty, sweet beers like stouts, porters, and many craft styles tend to have more leftover carbohydrate than light lagers. Higher-alcohol beers also mean more alcohol per glass, which is harder on the gut lining.

**Volume.** The simplest factor of all. A night on beer often means two to four liters of carbonated liquid going into your stomach. That alone stretches the stomach and adds to the feeling of bloat. We look at the broader effects in our article on [beer hangovers](/never-hungover/beer-hangover).

## Food Intolerances That Show Up When You Drink

Sometimes alcohol isn't the main problem. It just shows up alongside an intolerance that was already there.

- **Lactose intolerance.** Cream liqueurs, White Russians, eggnog, and mudslides contain dairy. If milk normally gives you gas, these will too, and alcohol won't make it easier. A lactase enzyme tablet taken with the first creamy drink may help, or simply pick a different cocktail.
- **Fructose malabsorption.** Cider, sweet wines, and drinks made with high-fructose corn syrup or a lot of fruit juice can cause gas and loose stools in people who don't absorb fructose well.
- **Gluten.** Covered above under beer.
- **Histamine sensitivity.** Wine, especially red, and some beers contain histamine, and alcohol may make it harder for some people to break histamine down. This more often shows up as flushing, a stuffy nose, or headaches, but some people notice gut symptoms too. See our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) for more.
- **Sugar alcohols in "low-sugar" mixers.** Some sugar-free mixers and diet drinks use sweeteners like sorbitol or other sugar alcohols, which are known to cause gas and loose stools in larger amounts. Check the label if a "light" drink seems to cause more trouble than a regular one.

## How to Get Rid of Gas After Drinking

If you're already gassy and uncomfortable, these are sensible, low-risk steps. None of them is a cure, and the gas will pass on its own, but they can make the wait easier.

1. **Move around.** A 10 to 20 minute walk is one of the most reliable ways to help trapped gas move through. Gentle stretching or simply getting up and around works too.
2. **Drink still water, not more bubbles.** Water helps with dehydration and keeps things moving. Avoid soda, sparkling water, and "hair of the dog" beer, which just adds more gas.
3. **Try simethicone for trapped bubbles.** Over-the-counter products containing simethicone (Gas-X is a well-known brand) work by making small gas bubbles merge into larger ones that are easier to pass. It isn't absorbed into the body, and there's no known interaction with alcohol. It works best for the bubbly, pressure type of gas rather than odor or cramping.
4. **Peppermint tea or ginger.** Peppermint relaxes the smooth muscle of the gut, and peppermint oil capsules have reasonable evidence for easing bloating in irritable bowel syndrome. One caution: peppermint can also relax the valve at the top of your stomach, so skip it if heartburn is part of your hangover. Ginger is a gentler option that many people find settles nausea too.
5. **Eat bland, easy food.** Toast, rice, bananas, oats, plain chicken, or eggs are less likely to add fuel than greasy fried food, beans, onions, or a big pile of fruit. Small portions are better than one large meal.
6. **Use a warm compress.** A heating pad or hot water bottle on your belly can ease cramping and make you more comfortable while the gas passes.
7. **Give it time.** Most post-drinking gas settles within a day as the alcohol clears and your gut calms down.

**What about Pepto-Bismol?** Bismuth subsalicylate can help with an upset stomach and loose stools, and there is some research suggesting bismuth can reduce sulfur odor in gas. But it contains a salicylate, a relative of aspirin, so it shouldn't be combined with aspirin, it isn't recommended for people allergic to aspirin, and it carries the same stomach-bleeding caution as other aspirin-type products for people who drink heavily. It can also turn your tongue and stool black, which is harmless but alarming if you don't expect it. Follow the label.

**What about activated charcoal?** It's sold for gas, but the evidence that it meaningfully reduces gas is mixed, and it can interfere with the absorption of medicines you take at the same time. It's not a great first choice.

**What about painkillers?** Gas isn't usually something painkillers fix. If you take something for a headache, remember that ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated, so take them with food and stick to the label dose.

## How to Prevent Gas When You Drink

Prevention works better than cure here, and most of it is simple.

- **Pick still drinks over fizzy ones.** Wine, or a spirit with still water, ice, or a little juice, puts far less gas in your stomach than beer, seltzer, or soda mixers.
- **If you love beer, choose lighter, clearer styles** and drink fewer of them. Alternate with water rather than another pint.
- **Pour into a glass and skip the straw.** You'll swallow less air.
- **Slow down.** Fast drinking means more swallowed air, more alcohol hitting your gut at once, and usually more total drinks.
- **Eat a proper meal before you start.** Drinking on an empty stomach is harder on the stomach lining and tends to make every gut symptom worse. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why.
- **Go easy on the classic gas foods** during the night: beans, onions, garlic-heavy dishes, big portions of fried food, and sugary snacks.
- **Watch the sweet mixers.** Swap cola or sugary syrups for soda water, still water with lime, or a small splash of juice.
- **Know your own triggers.** If you notice that cider wrecks you but wine doesn't, or that creamy cocktails always lead to a rough night, that's useful information. A quick note in your phone after a night out can reveal a pattern in a few weeks.
- **Don't smoke or vape while drinking.** Besides everything else, it pulls air into your stomach.

## Gas After Drinking Every Time: When It Might Be Something Else

For most people, gas after drinking is a predictable reaction to bubbles, sugars, and a busy night. A few patterns are worth taking more seriously.

- **You get gas, bloating, or diarrhea after only one or two drinks**, or after most meals as well. That can point to irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, an intolerance, or bacterial overgrowth, all of which a doctor can help sort out.
- **Beer is always the problem, but wine and spirits aren't.** Consider gluten. Ask about celiac testing before changing your diet.
- **You also flush, get a stuffy nose, or a racing heart quickly after drinking.** That can be alcohol intolerance, often due to differences in how your body breaks down alcohol or histamine.
- **You drink most days and you're bloated most of the time.** Regular heavy drinking is linked to changes in the gut and can affect the liver and pancreas. A swollen belly that keeps growing, together with yellowing of the skin or eyes, needs prompt medical attention, because fluid in the abdomen can be a sign of liver disease rather than gas.
- **Upper belly pain that spreads to your back**, especially with nausea or vomiting after a heavy session, can be pancreatitis. That needs urgent care, not a gas remedy.

None of these is meant to alarm you. They're simply the situations where "it's just the beer" stops being the most likely explanation, and a quick conversation with a doctor is the sensible move.

## Where DHM Fits In (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that some people take to support their body when they drink. Most of the research on it comes from lab and animal studies, which suggest it may help the body process alcohol and may protect the liver, along with limited human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that DHM reduces gas, bloating, or any other gut symptom from drinking. It won't take the bubbles out of a beer or stop your gut bacteria from fermenting a basket of fries.

If you're interested in DHM for the broader hangover picture, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For gas specifically, the changes in this article, such as fewer bubbles, fewer sweet mixers, slower drinking, and better food, will do far more.

## The Bottom Line

Gas after drinking usually comes from carbonation you swallow during the night and fermentation of sugars and starches in your gut the next day, made worse by alcohol's effect on the gut lining and by swallowed air. Beer, cider, and sweet fizzy cocktails are the most common culprits, and still drinks are the easiest swap. A walk, water, bland food, and simethicone can help while it passes. If gas comes with severe pain, a hard swollen belly, vomiting, blood, black stools, or fever, or if it happens even with small amounts of alcohol, see a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get so gassy after drinking alcohol?**

Usually because of a mix of causes. Carbonated drinks like beer, seltzer, and soda mixers put carbon dioxide straight into your stomach. Beer, cider, and sweet cocktails contain sugars and starches that your gut bacteria ferment into gas hours later. Alcohol also irritates the gut lining and changes how quickly food moves through, and fast drinking, talking, straws, and smoking make you swallow extra air. Late-night food like fries, pizza, and beans adds even more.

**Why do I have gas the morning after drinking?**

Next-morning gas is mostly produced in your large intestine. Sugars and starches from beer, cider, sweet mixers, and bar food that your small intestine didn't absorb reach your colon overnight, where bacteria ferment them and release gas. Alcohol can also irritate the gut and make digestion less efficient, which sends more material down to be fermented. It usually settles within a day.

**Does beer cause more gas than other alcohol?**

For most people, yes. Beer is carbonated, you drink it in large volumes, and it still contains leftover carbohydrates from the grain that gut bacteria can ferment. Heavier, sweeter, and unfiltered styles tend to be worse than light lagers. Beer also contains gluten, which causes gas and bloating in people with celiac disease and in some people who are sensitive to wheat and barley.

**What alcohol causes the least gas?**

Spirits served neat, on ice, or with still water or a small splash of juice are the least likely to cause gas from the drink itself, followed by dry still wine. Soda water has no sugar but is still carbonated, so a vodka soda can still make you burp. Sweet mixers, cider, beer, and creamy cocktails (if you're lactose intolerant) are the most likely to cause trouble.

**How do I get rid of gas after drinking?**

Take a 10 to 20 minute walk, drink still water instead of anything fizzy, and eat bland food in small portions. Over-the-counter simethicone (such as Gas-X) can help trapped bubbles pass and has no known interaction with alcohol. Peppermint or ginger tea and a warm compress can ease cramping, though skip peppermint if you also have heartburn. Most post-drinking gas clears on its own within a day.

**Why does my gas smell so bad after drinking?**

Most gas is odorless. The smell comes from small amounts of sulfur-containing gases that bacteria make when they break down certain foods, such as meat, eggs, cheese, onions, garlic, and cruciferous vegetables, plus sulfur compounds in some beers. A night of drinking usually means more of those foods and more fermentation overall. Bad-smelling gas alone isn't a warning sign, but pale, greasy stools or weight loss alongside it are worth mentioning to a doctor.

**Is gas and bloating after drinking a sign of something serious?**

Usually not. It's a common, short-lived reaction to carbonation, sugars, and gut irritation. See a doctor promptly if you have severe or worsening belly pain, pain spreading to your back with vomiting, a hard swollen abdomen, vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, fever, or you can't pass gas or stool. Book a regular appointment if you get gas and bloating after only one or two drinks, or if it's constant and you drink most days.

**Can alcohol cause gas and diarrhea together?**

Yes. Alcohol can speed up movement through the intestines and irritate the gut lining, so less water and food is absorbed. More undigested material reaches the colon, which leads to both looser stools and more fermentation gas. This usually passes within a day or two. Diarrhea lasting longer than that, or with blood, fever, or signs of dehydration, needs medical attention.

**Does DHM help with gas after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM reduces gas or bloating from drinking. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. For gas, the most effective changes are practical ones: fewer carbonated drinks, fewer sweet mixers, slower drinking, and lighter food.
